analysis.one_liner: Taxes Wall Street securities trades 0.25% to fund job creation and cut the deficit.
analysis.headline: The bill was never acted on after its Senate referral, dying in the Finance Committee with only three cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a 0.25% excise tax on most stock, bond, and derivatives trades, raising money the bill says would fund job creation and deficit reduction. It is written to spare ordinary savers: trades inside 401(k)s, IRAs, 529 college and health savings accounts, and mutual funds are exempt, and individuals get a credit rebating up to $250 ($500 per married couple) of the tax each year. High-frequency and hedging trades would pay a reduced 0.02% rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit twice: retirement, education, and health savings accounts are exempt from the tax entirely, and anyone who does pay it gets a credit back for up to $250 ($500 per couple). The revenue is earmarked for job creation and deficit reduction, which spreads the benefit broadly.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 0.25% excise tax on the fair market value of traded stocks, publicly traded debt, partnership interests, and derivatives, including credit default swaps, aimed at high-volume Wall Street trading. [S2] [S3]
Exempts trades inside 401(a), 403(b), IRA, 529, and health savings accounts, and exempts mutual fund purchases, so ordinary people's retirement and college savings are not taxed. [S2] [S3]
Gives every individual a credit against the tax worth up to $250 ($500 for married couples filing jointly) per year, covering the tax on most small investors' trades entirely. [S2] [S3]
States the tax is to fund job creation and deficit reduction, and taxes short-term debt instruments and hedging transactions at a lower 0.02% rate. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large securities dealers, high-frequency trading firms, and wealthy investors who trade outside exempt accounts pay the tax; exchanges, brokers, and trading facilities are made responsible for collecting and remitting it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wall Street trading firms and exchanges

drawbacks.text: Trading costs can be passed through, so investors who hold stocks and bonds outside exempt accounts — taxable brokerage accounts — would bear some of the tax despite the credit cap. [S3]

A unilateral U.S. trading tax could push some trading volume to foreign exchanges, which is why the bill directs the Treasury Secretary to write rules preventing avoidance through non-U.S. persons, but those rules were never drafted or tested. [S3]

Because the tax hits all trades regardless of frequency, long-term investors in taxable accounts pay it on every purchase; the bill's reduced 0.02% hedging rate also means the highest-volume traders pay proportionally less per dollar traded. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is careful about small savers: exempting retirement, education, and health accounts and rebating up to $250 per person removes most of the burden on ordinary people, while the burden falls on high-volume trading. The main uncertainty is whether some tax cost leaks into prices paid by taxable-account investors and whether trading moves offshore, which the bill tries to address but never got the chance to test.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended. [S1] [S5]

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on December 23, 2009, with Senators Sanders, Whitehouse, and Brown as original cosponsors. [S1] [S3]
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, and the congressional record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote. [S1] [S5]
The bill ended with just three cosponsors: 2 of 58 Senate Democrats and the chamber's sole Independent. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wall Street trading firms and exchanges are better off because the tax never advanced; no one else gains from the bill's failure.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; Sanders is listed as the chamber's sole Independent and Whitehouse and Brown as 2 of 58 Senate Democrats.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it; the record shows no committee action.

against.name: Securities and derivatives trading industry
against.role: Firms, exchanges, and high-frequency traders who would pay the tax
against.what_they_did: Opposed securities transaction taxes during the post-crisis debate; the bill attracted no Republican cosponsors and few Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no voting record exists; its only support was 2 of 58 Senate Democrats plus the chamber's one Independent, with no Republican cosponsors. [S4]

industries.industry: Securities exchanges, brokers, and high-frequency trading firms
industries.note: They would owe or collect the 0.25% tax on every covered trade, with the cost falling heaviest on high-volume trading. The bill's revenue is aimed at jobs and deficit reduction that benefit the broader public.
Credit default swaps, options, and other derivatives are explicitly taxed at 0.25% of notional value, though hedging trades get a reduced 0.02% rate.

industries.industry: Mutual fund companies and retirement plan administrators
industries.note: Their products — mutual funds, 401(k)s, IRAs, 529 plans — are exempt from the tax, making them the protected, tax-free channel for ordinary savers' investments.
